result:
There is a specific kind of silence that lives inside things that are working.

Not the silence of emptiness, but the silence of function. The refrigerator humming so evenly you forget it’s there. The bridge you drive over every morning without ever thinking about the bridge. The friendship that doesn’t need constant checking-in because the foundation is solid. We don’t notice these things precisely because they are doing their job. And I’ve been thinking a lot lately about how much of our lives, and our praise, is pointed in the wrong direction.

We celebrate the builders. We love the creators, the innovators, the founders, the artists who make something from nothing. We put them on stages and give them awards and write profiles about their moment of inspiration. The narrative we love is: Before, there was nothing. After, there was something. It’s dramatic. It’s clean. It has a clear beginning.

We almost never celebrate the maintainers.

And yet, maintenance is most of life.

Think about it. For every hour spent building a house, there are ten thousand hours spent living in it, fixing the leaky faucet, repainting the walls where the sun has faded them, sweeping the leaves out of the gutters, replacing the broken tile. For every brilliant novel written, there are decades of readers keeping it alive by remembering it, teaching it, pressing it into a friend’s hands and saying, “You have to read this.” For every new piece of software launched with confetti and a press release, there are years of quiet, unglamorous work patching bugs, updating dependencies, answering support tickets at 2 a.m. because a server went down.

Creation is a spark. Maintenance is the long, slow work of keeping the fire lit.

I used to think this made maintenance boring. Less important. Secondary. Now I think it might be the other way around. Creation is relatively easy. Anyone can have an idea in the shower. Anyone can be struck by inspiration for a few incandescent minutes. But to stay? To tend? To return again and again to the same thing and care for it even when it is no longer new or exciting? That takes a different kind of devotion.

There is a Japanese concept I love called *kintsugi*, the art of repairing broken pottery with seams of gold. The philosophy behind it is that the breakage and repair are not something to hide, but part of the history of the object, something that makes it more beautiful. The bowl is more valuable after it has been broken and tended to. But we often treat our own lives as if we should be constantly replacing the bowl instead of mending it.

Entropy is the quiet law that governs everything. It’s the scientific term for the tendency of all ordered things to slide toward disorder. Your room gets messy on its own; it never gets cleaner on its own. Your body ages. Your relationships drift if you don’t water them. Your knowledge fades. The garden grows weeds without any encouragement at all. The universe, left to its own devices, prefers mess.

Maintenance is the human act of saying: not today. Not this corner of the universe. Here, I will push back against entropy for a little while.

A friend of mine is a bridge inspector. He gets up before dawn and drives out to bridges in the middle of nowhere, bridges most people will never know the name of, and he crawls under them with a flashlight and a clipboard. He taps the concrete and listens. He measures rust. He writes reports that almost no one will read unless something goes wrong. When he does his job perfectly, nothing happens. No one dies, no bridge collapses, no news story airs. His success is invisible. I asked him once if that bothers him, that his best work is the absence of a disaster. He laughed and said, “That’s all work if you do it right.”

That stuck with me.

Consider what we might call “maintenance work” in human life:

There is the maintenance of the body — not the dramatic transformation, not the before-and-after photo, but the daily walk, the glass of water, the sleep you prioritize, the stretching when your back is stiff. It’s not Instagrammable. It doesn’t get applause. But it is the reason you can still move through the world without pain ten years from now.

There is the maintenance of a home — washing the dishes again, knowing they will be dirty again tomorrow. Folding the laundry. Wiping down the counters. It can feel Sisyphean, rolling the same boulder up the same hill every day. But Albert Camus, who wrote about Sisyphus, said we must imagine him happy. Perhaps the point was never to get to the top and be done. Perhaps the point is the care in the rolling itself.

There is the maintenance of knowledge — re-reading the book you thought you already understood, realizing you missed half of it. Taking notes again. Staying a student even after the world has decided you are an expert.

And there is the maintenance of love — which might be the most important and most invisible of all. Love at the beginning is fireworks, all dopamine and novelty. Love after five or ten or fifty years is mostly maintenance. It’s remembering how she takes her coffee. It’s asking about his mother’s appointment. It’s apologizing even when you are tired. It’s choosing to listen, again, to the same story because it matters to them. It’s not grand gestures, but a thousand small, almost unseen acts of tending. The ion that holds a relationship together is not passion, but consideration repeated until it becomes a habit.

We live in a culture that is addicted to the new. New phones, new apps, new trends, new selves. We are encouraged to constantly disrupt, pivot, rebrand, optimize. We treat boredom as a failure and stability as stagnation. To stay with something, to maintain it, can feel like you are being left behind.

But what if staying is the most radical thing you can do?

I think about old-growth forests. A forest isn’t just a collection of trees that sprouted up overnight. It’s a network that has been maintained for centuries by fungi and roots and decaying leaves and beetles and birds. The oldest trees are not the most impressive because they grew the fastest, but because they endured. They survived fires and droughts and storms. Their rings are records of maintenance through time.

Or think about the great cathedrals of Europe. They took generations to build. No single architect saw one finished. The man who laid the first stone knew he would never see the spire. He was building for a future he would not inhabit. And then, for the next eight hundred years, other people have maintained them — replacing stones, fixing stained glass after wars, sweeping the floors. The cathedral exists not because one genius created it, but because thousands of ordinary people agreed, century after century, that it was worth keeping.

That’s the thing about maintenance: it is an act of faith in the future. You clean the kitchen tonight because you believe there will be a morning and you will want to eat breakfast here. You save money because you believe your future self will need it. You are kind to your child even on the hard days because you believe that kindness compounds into a person.

So much of our anxiety comes from feeling like we have to constantly make something impressive and new to justify our existence. But maybe the question is not “What did you create today?” Maybe the question is “What did you quietly keep from falling apart today?”

Did you keep a promise? Did you keep a plant alive? Did you keep your temper when it would have been easier to snap? Did you keep trying at something that is difficult and slow?

That is a life.

I’m learning to look for the maintainers and thank them. The janitor who has kept my office building clean for twelve years and knows which door sticks when it rains. The open-source programmer who has quietly updated the same library for a decade so that half the internet doesn’t break. The neighbor who shovels the snow from the shared driveway without being asked. My mother, who has kept every birthday card I ever made her.

Their work hums in the background, like a refrigerator, like a love, like a forest.

If you are one of those people — if your days feel repetitive, if your work feels unseen, if you wonder whether all that small, repeated effort matters — it does. It is the only thing that has ever mattered.

The world is not kept alive by the few spectacular moments of creation. It is kept alive by the many, quiet, stubborn acts of care that happen every single day, without fanfare, without audience.

And that might be the most beautiful kind of work there is.
